lesson.title: How much energy a circuit moves
lesson.orientation: Watch the calculated current as you raise the supply, and keep track of how hard the resistor is working.

visualBrief.learningPurpose: Show one resistor with its voltage and current marked, which are the two values a power calculation needs.
facts: Power is the product of current and potential difference.
The circuit is a single closed path.
The resistor value and the supply voltage fix the current.
visualBrief.altTextDraft: A battery and a single resistor in a closed loop, with the supply voltage and the calculated current both labelled.
verificationChecks: The current shown agrees with the voltage divided by the resistance.

lesson.reviewLabel: Power and energy in a circuit
lesson.nextAction: Open the last lesson to meet a component that does not obey Ohm's law.

steps.headline: Power is energy transferred each second: current times voltage.

lead.text: Power is the rate of transferring energy, in watts (W). One watt is one joule each second. Over a time t, a component transfers energy E = P × t.
Use I in amperes and V in volts, and P comes out in watts.
Two resistors in the same circuit. The first carries 0.5 A with 8 V across it. The second carries 2 A with 2 V across it.

reveal.text: They transfer the same power. You multiplied each pair: both come to 4 W.

steps.headline: Ohm's law lets you write power from whichever two quantities you know.

lead.text: Put V = IR into P = IV. Or put I = V/R in. Either way you only need two quantities.

steps.headline: A 12 V supply drives 0.5 A through a heater. Find the power.

workedSteps.text: Write power in terms of current and voltage.

steps.headline: A 9 V supply drives 20 mA through a component. Find the power.

workedSteps.text: Write power in terms of current and voltage.
Convert the current to amperes: 1 mA is 0.001 A.
Multiply by the voltage, in watts.

lead.text: You know the voltage and the resistance. Pick the form of the power equation that uses them.

reveal.text: With voltage and resistance, P = V² ÷ R skips the current. You could also find the current first and use P = IV.

lead.text: Power is a rate, so how much energy gets transferred depends on how long the circuit runs.

blocks.text: A battery gives each coulomb of charge 4 joules. Each second, 0.5 coulombs pass through it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the power of a component from its current and voltage, and turn power into energy.

recap.keyIdea: Power is the rate of energy transfer: current times voltage, in watts. Energy is power multiplied by the time the circuit runs.

blocks.text: You found that 0.5 A at 8 V and 2 A at 2 V transfer the same power, and that a 100 Ω resistor with 5 V across it transfers 0.25 W.

recap.nextHook: Every component so far obeyed Ohm's law. Meet one that doesn't.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between the power a resistor dissipates and the energy it transfers.
hints: One of the two quantities depends on how long the circuit runs.
Think about what has to be multiplied by time.
State the relationship between the two quantities in one sentence.

rejectedIdeas: power and energy are the same
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts. Energy is power multiplied by the time the circuit runs, so a 0.25 W resistor transfers 15 J in 60 s.

questions.onCorrect: Power is the rate of transfer in watts. Energy is power times the time it runs.

questions.prompt: A resistor carries a current of 0.25 A with 6 V across it. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: Power uses both the current and the voltage.
Write P = IV and substitute the two values.
Multiply 0.25 by 6.
questions.onCorrect: 1.5 W. Current times voltage gives power in watts.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the voltage by the current, which gives a resistance, not a power.
Adding the two numbers mixes different quantities. Power is their product.

questions.prompt: A 100 Ω resistor has 5 V across it. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: You know the voltage and the resistance. Which quantity is missing for P = IV?
Find the current with I = V / R, then use it in P = IV.
Or use P = V² / R: square the voltage, then divide by 100.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: I = 5 V / 100 Ω = 0.05 A, so P = IV = 0.05 A × 5 V = 0.25 W. Equivalently P = V² / R = 25 / 100 = 0.25 W.

questions.onCorrect: 0.25 W. Voltage and resistance are enough: P = V² ÷ R.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the current. Power needs the voltage as well.
That multiplies the voltage by the resistance, which is not a power.
That is the voltage squared on its own. Divide by the resistance.

questions.prompt: A 9 V supply drives 20 mA through a component. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: Convert the current to amperes before multiplying.
1 mA is 0.001 A.
Multiply the converted current by the voltage.
questions.onCorrect: 0.18 W. Convert milliamperes to amperes first, then multiply by the voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses 20 as if it were amperes. Milliamperes are a thousandth of an ampere.

questions.prompt: How many joules does the battery deliver each second?
hints: Each coulomb brings 4 joules. How many coulombs pass in one second?
Half a coulomb brings half of 4 joules.
Work out 4 × 0.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each second 0.5 coulombs pass, each carrying 4 J: 0.5 × 4 = 2 J.

questions.onCorrect: 2 J each second. Energy per coulomb times coulombs per second gives energy per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the 0.5. Half a coulomb carries less energy than a whole one, so the answer is smaller than 4.
Adding mixes two different things. Each coulomb brings energy, so scale that energy by how many coulombs pass.

hints: Power uses both current and voltage.
Work out the product for each resistor.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They transfer the same power: 0.5 A × 8 V and 2 A × 2 V both give 4 W.

choices.label: The first, with 0.5 A and 8 V
The second, with 2 A and 2 V

questions.onCorrect: Same power: both products come to 4 W. Neither current nor voltage alone tells you how hard a component works.

misconceptions.feedback: It has more voltage but less current. Compare the products, not one number at a time.
It has more current but less voltage. Compare the products, not one number at a time.

questions.prompt: Why can you multiply the current by the voltage to find power?
hints: Think back to the coulombs and joules in the opening puzzle.
What units does the product of coulombs per second and joules per coulomb have?

acceptedIdeas: Voltage is energy per coulomb and current is coulombs per second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Voltage is energy per coulomb and current is coulombs per second, so the product is energy per second.

choices.label: Voltage is energy per coulomb and current is coulombs per second
Multiplying always gives the larger of the two numbers
Current and voltage are two names for the same thing

questions.onCorrect: Joules per coulomb times coulombs per second is joules per second, which is watts.

misconceptions.feedback: Multiplying doesn't pick the larger number. Think about what each quantity measures.
They are different quantities. One counts charge passing, the other measures the energy each charge carries.

questions.prompt: A 9 V supply drives 0.2 A through a lamp for 60 s. How much energy does the lamp transfer, in joules?
hints: Find the power first, from the current and the voltage.
Power is energy each second. How many seconds does the lamp run?
Multiply the power by the 60 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 108 J. Power gives joules each second, and the lamp runs for 60 of them.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the power, joules each second. The lamp runs for a whole minute.
Power is already a rate, so you multiply by time, not divide.
That leaves out the voltage. Find the power first.

questions.prompt: A 50 Ω resistor carries 0.1 A. Calculate the power it transfers, in watts.
hints: You know the current and the resistance, not the voltage.
Find the voltage across the resistor with V = IR, or use P = I²R.
Square the current, then multiply by the resistance.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5 W. With current and resistance, P = I²R gives the power directly.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the voltage across the resistor. Power needs one more step.
That is the current squared. Multiply by the resistance as well.

questions.prompt: A heater transfers 100 joules of energy every second. What is its power, in watts?
hints: A watt is one joule each second.
How many joules each second does the heater transfer?
Read the power straight from the joules each second.
questions.onCorrect: 100 W. A watt is one joule each second.

misconceptions.feedback: A watt is one joule each second, so the number is not divided down.
Power in joules each second needs no extra multiplying.

questions.prompt: You know a resistor's voltage and its resistance. Which expression gives its power?
hints: Think about what the step just said.
Which option matches it?
questions.onCorrect: V² ÷ R. It uses exactly the two quantities you know.

misconceptions.feedback: That needs the current, which you don't have yet.
That is the current, not the power.
